newsitem.title: USA: CLINTON AIDE SEES "DIFFICULT VOTE" ON FAST TRACK.
newsitem.headline: CLINTON AIDE SEES "DIFFICULT VOTE" ON FAST TRACK.

text.p: President Bill Clinton faces a major challenge this fall persuading Congress to allow him to persue new trade agreements using "fast-track" negotiating authority, a senior administration aide said Thursday.
"I think it will be a difficult vote," said the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
Many members of Congress question the need for additional trade pacts, despite the importance of exports to the U.S. economy, he acknowledged.
Whatever the odds, the adminstration will push for a vote in both the House and Senate this year.

"If there's reasons you can't get it done in 1997, it's hard to think you'll be better off in 1998" when the entire House and one-third of the Senate will be occupied with upcoming elections, he said.
On Wednesday, Clinton identified fast track approval as one of his top priorities for the rest of 1997.
Approval would allow the administration, "to continue to open more foreign markets through tough, fair trade agreements," Clinton said.
When Congress grants fast track, it gives up its right to amend any trade agreements negotiated by the administration. Instead, it can only vote yes or no on the overall pact.
Key Democrats have insisted that any fast track legislation also require the administration to negotiate labor and environmental agreements to accompany the trade pacts.
However, Republicans oppose granting that authority because they fear such pacts could stifle trade.
The divergent views present a quandry for the administration, which hopes to craft a package this month that will capture enough bipartisan support for approval.

"We haven't done a vote count" to see just how much support for fast track already exists, the official said. "We're going to have to have Republicans and Democrats. What the exact number is (of each) I don't know."

The administration wants fast-track authority most immediately to negotiate a trade agreement with Chile, which already has separate pacts with Canada and Mexico -- the United States' partners in the North American Free Trade Agreement. But it also hopes to expand NAFTA into a free trade pact covering all of North and South America; persue separate trade negotiations with Asian-Pacific nations; and conduct further global negotiations under the World Trade Organization.
Many members of Congress have come to believe that trade pacts benefit other nations far more the United States.
The Clinton administration disputes that view, but it acknowledges it exists and will work hard to convince members otherwise, the adminstration aide said.
